title: When Peer Review Does Not Reach Closure: Generative AI, Critique Inflation, and the Editorial Stopping Problem
content: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) makes candidate criticism inexpensive to produce, while verification, revision, and editorial attention remain costly. A manuscript may consequently improve across revision rounds even as the volume of critique fails to decrease. We define critique inflation as growth or persistence in candidate or optional critique without a corresponding increase in material deficiencies. A theoretical framework distinguishes verified material concerns, verified non-blocking improvements, and invalid or unsubstantiated candidates. Raw comment counts can depend on the critique prompt as well as on manuscript deficiencies. An editorial selectivity condition shows that, under a positive lower bound on per-comment response burden, bounded non-material author burden requires the fraction of optional comments converted into mandatory requests to scale at most inversely with their supply. The revision model \( D_{k+1}=\rho D_k+u_k \) yields a threshold \( u^\star=(1-\rho)\varepsilon \) for newly added mandatory load. A uniform bound below this threshold guarantees finite-time entry into the acceptance region of the model; persistent load at or above it can prevent entry. Verified decisive objections retain their scientific force independently of their provenance. The framework provides operational indicators and motivates testable hypotheses for multi-round, AI-assisted peer review.
